nary_nodes.label: Euclid discovers oldest quasars
evidence: The Euclid space telescope has spotted the oldest quasars — the brightest objects in the universe — ever discovered, deepening a cosmic mystery that has been puzzling scientists.

In a study published on Monday, an international team of astronomers announced they had discovered 31 quasars, including the two oldest observed yet, using the European Space Agency's Euclid telescope, which is at a stable hovering spot around 1.5 million kilometers from Earth.

nary_nodes.label: Euclid transformed quasar hunting
evidence: Previous quasar hunts were mostly carried out with ground-based telescopes, but the launch of Euclid in 2023 "has transformed this field," Daming Yang, the lead author of the study in Astronomy & Astrophysics, told AFP.

nary_nodes.label: Euclid doubled known ancient quasars
evidence: In just two years, Euclid has doubled the number of ancient quasars known to science, added Yang, a PhD student at Leiden University in the Netherlands.

nary_nodes.label: Euclid is a game-changer for quasar hunting
evidence: "Euclid is a true game-changer," Yang said in a statement.

"Before, we could only find a handful of the very brightest ancient quasars, but Euclid lets us search far more efficiently across huge areas of sky to capture much fainter light. It's a unique tool for quasar hunting."

nary_nodes.label: Quasars used as lighthouses to study reionization
evidence: "We can use quasars as a lighthouse to study the gas between us and them, so that we can trace how the universe was reionized through this cosmic history," Daming Yang said.

nary_nodes.label: Cosmic objects bigger than expected
evidence: The quasars are also the latest example of a problem that has been increasingly baffling scientists.
As more powerful telescopes allow us to see further back in time, galaxies and other cosmic objects have turned out to be far bigger than had been thought possible at such an early age.

nary_nodes.label: Puzzle becomes more perplexing
evidence: "Every step further back in time makes the puzzle more perplexing," study co-author Joseph Hennawi said in a statement about the newly discovered quasars.

nary_nodes.label: Massive black holes existed in early universe
evidence: "These monsters -- weighing billions of times the mass of our sun -- somehow already existed when the universe was in its infancy," he said.
"We don't yet have a good understanding of how they grew so massive, so fast."

nary_nodes.label: Scientists search for even older quasars
evidence: Hoping to find an answer, the scientists are searching for even older quasars.

nary_nodes.label: James Webb observed newly announced quasars
evidence: The far-seeing James Webb space telescope also recently observed the newly announced quasars, Daming said, and the team will soon begin sifting through the data it collected.

nary_nodes.label: Team sifting through James Webb data
evidence: The far-seeing James Webb space telescope also recently observed the newly announced quasars, Daming said, and the team will soon begin sifting through the data it collected.

nary_nodes.label: Team hopes to stitch quasar chronicle
evidence: The team eventually hope to stitch together "a quasar chronicle of the first billion years," Hennawi said.

nary_nodes.label: Euclid telescope launched
evidence: Launched from Cape Canaveral on July 1, 2023 atop a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, the $1.5 billion Euclid is stationed about a million miles from Earth on the far side of the moon's orbit.

nary_nodes.label: Euclid mission to chart sky
evidence: Euclid launched in 2023 on a mission to chart one-third of the sky in the hopes of shedding light on the enduring mysteries of dark matter and dark energy.

nary_nodes.label: Euclid captured largest photo of galaxy's heart
evidence: Just last month, scientists announced the Euclid telescope had captured the largest and most detailed photo ever taken of our galaxy's crowded heart, a dazzling image packed with 60 million stars, the European Space Agency said Wednesday.

nary_nodes.label: Euclid captured photos of cosmos in 2024
evidence: In 2024, Euclid captured dazzling photos of the cosmos, including an image of a massive cluster of galaxies called Abell 2390.

nary_nodes.label: Euclid captured image of Abell 2390
evidence: In 2024, Euclid captured dazzling photos of the cosmos, including an image of a massive cluster of galaxies called Abell 2390.

nary_nodes.label: Euclid captured Perseus galaxy cluster image in 2023
evidence: Another jaw-dropping image, captured in 2023, provides a spectacular wide-angle view of the Perseus galaxy cluster, revealing at least 1,000 gravitationally-bound galaxies with another 100,000 or so sprinkled across the more distant background — many of them never before seen.

nary_nodes.label: Euclid monitors galaxies and clusters
evidence: Over the course of its six-year mission, the observatory will image the entire sky around the Milky Way, monitoring galaxies and galaxy clusters dating back 10 billion years.
